content_units: You want the fastest path to being interview-ready while studying part-time, with hard limits of   5 hours/week   and   $600 total  . On those priorities,   Course B is the better overall fit   because it stays within your weekly time limit and adds   Python + statistics  , which close more common entry-level skill gaps.
Course A is faster in calendar time and stronger on portfolio volume, but it   exceeds your weekly cap   at 6 hours/week.
Course   Length   Weekly Time   Total Cost   Core Skills   Projects   Fit With Your Constraints   Interview Readiness
Course A   8 weeks   6 hrs/week   $420   Excel, SQL, Tableau   4     Fails time limit     Faster portfolio building; weaker on Python/stats
Course B   14 weeks   4 hrs/week   $560   Excel, SQL, Python, statistics   2     Fits fully     Broader analyst foundation; slower timeline
Best fit for you   —   —   —   —   —     Course B     Better balance of realism, employability, and sustainability
-   Meets your schedule  : 4 hours/week is under your 5-hour limit.
-   Stays in budget  : $560 is within your $600 cap.
-   Stronger long-term skill mix  : Excel + SQL + Python + statistics is closer to many analyst job postings than Excel + SQL + Tableau alone.
-   Safer for moderate math confidence  : the slower pace gives you more room to absorb statistics without overload.

-   Better for career transition  : your retail operations background pairs well with data cleaning, reporting, KPI tracking, and process analysis; Python/statistics help you sound more credible in interviews.
Why you might still choose it:
-   Interview-ready sooner on the calendar  : 8 weeks instead of 14.
-   More portfolio pieces  : 4 projects can help if you need resume material quickly.
-   Tableau is very visible in analyst hiring  .
-   6 hours/week breaks your limit  , so it is the riskier choice for consistency and completion.
If “sooner” means   earliest possible calendar finish  , then   Course A   wins.
If “sooner” means   realistically finishable without burnout and more aligned to common analyst screening skills  , then   Course B   is the better answer.
For your exact constraints, the strongest recommendation is:
Choose Course B, then self-study Tableau and build 1 extra dashboard project alongside it.
- and enough presentation/visualization work to discuss in interviews.
Skills You’ll Still Need to Self-Study
-   Tableau or Power BI   — many entry-level analyst roles expect at least one BI/dashboard tool.
-   Business storytelling  : how to explain insights clearly to non-technical stakeholders.
-   Portfolio presentation  : project writeups with business question, dataset, method, result, and recommendation.
-   Basic KPI design  : conversion rate, retention, sales per store, inventory turns, margin, forecasting basics.
-   Interview SQL practice  : joins, aggregations, CASE WHEN, window functions if possible.
These gaps matter because many analyst interviews test not just dashboards and SQL, but also whether you understand   why numbers change   and how to work with messier data.
Fastest Path to a Stronger Outcome
A good part-time plan with   Course B  :
- 1 mini dashboard from a retail-style dataset
-   By the end   aim to have:
- 1 polished resume bullet set tied to retail operations metrics
That combination should make you more interview-ready than Course B alone and more sustainable than forcing Course A.
